title: Seeking refuge first
hook: recitation begins with refuge from Shaytan, then bismillah (16:98)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tilawah, the Qur'an heard before it's read. Your line was hear it first. Today, the two short lines said before a recitation begins. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

A reciter in front of a packed hall, or a nine-year-old at an evening class in Ohio: before the first verse, there are usually two short lines, the same two. Reciters say them the way a pilot runs the checklist before takeoff, quietly, as part of starting. The first line isn't from the surah at all. It's a request for protection. The second is the bismillah, which you met on day one. So why does a recitation start by asking for shelter, and only then say the name?
screen: `TWO LINES BEFORE THE FIRST VERSE.` → `THE SAME TWO, EACH TIME.` → `SHELTER FIRST.`

segments.voice: The first line is called the ta'awwudh, from a root that means to seek refuge, to run to someone for cover. The usual words are a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim: I seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the rejected one. The habit comes from a verse in Surah an-Nahl, which Pickthall translates: And when thou recitest the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. Jurists debated whether that makes it required or strongly recommended; either way, it became the habit before recitation. Why ask for protection right before something good? Some Muslim teachers say the moment you turn toward the good is exactly when distraction arrives. Someone opens the text and suddenly remembers an email. Someone stands to pray and replays an argument. Muslims understand Shaytan as a real being who whispers, and some also see his work in that ordinary pull away from what matters. Either way, the ta'awwudh is a door closing behind you before you sit down. Then comes the bismillah: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Scholars point to the order. First you let go of what you don't want to bring in; then you name what you're entering with. Clearing, then naming. And the ta'awwudh travels beyond recitation. A hadith in Bukhari tells of two men quarreling near the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, one red in the face with anger. The Prophet said he knew words that would make the anger leave: a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim. So people say it before reciting, and also in the middle of a bad moment, when a thought won't let go.
screen: `TA'AWWUDH — TO RUN FOR COVER.` · `SEEK REFUGE WHEN YOU RECITE (16:98).` · `CLEAR FIRST, THEN NAME.` · `WORDS FOR A HOT MOMENT.` · then, large: `REFUGE, THEN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, say the two lines quietly, a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, then bismillah ir-rahman ir-rahim; if you don't, follow the shape: name one thing pulling at you, and set it down on a long out-breath. Then stay in the quiet that comes after clearing and naming, without reciting or planning.
Ta'awwudh. Seeking refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the line said before reciting, just before the bismillah. Today's word.
Your line: refuge, then the name. The door closes before you sit down. That's one hundred fifty-eight days.

howItsDone: Before reciting the Qur'an, Muslims usually say the ta'awwudh (a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim) and then, at the start of a surah, the bismillah; many also say the ta'awwudh when angry or troubled by a bad thought.

original.note: Arabic: seeking refuge, from the root '-w-dh, the same root as a'udhu, "I seek refuge."

trapdoor: what you thought: a warm-up line before the real recitation.
what it means: a request for shelter from Shaytan, clearing the way before the bismillah names what you begin with.
what a scholar hears: 16:98 grounds it; jurists debated whether it is required or strongly recommended; the root '-w-dh also opens Surahs 113 and 114: qul a'udhu.
